passages.text: Everest is the highest mountain in the world. But it isn’t next to the sea, so how was the measurement of 29,031 feet (8,848m) above sea level arrived at? And who first measured Mount Everest, and why? Mount Everest was measured using imaginary triangles and basic mathematics. Everest was measured by British surveyors, who figured out how high it was in 1854. The story of the Great Trigonometrical Survey started with tigers, camels, lost villages, elephants, goats, telescopes and surveying instruments. It ended with the discovery of the highest point on the earth’s surface. When the British got round to surveying the Himalayas they finally discovered Everest. It was a huge mountain hiding at the back that, when measured, proved to be higher than any other mountain in the world. But how did they know it was the highest mountain? You could hardly dangle a ruler down the side of Everest. So how was it done? The British in India decided to survey the land they had colonised, so they commissioned a Great Trigonometrical Survey in 1802. Imaginary triangles were to be drawn all over India, starting at the southern end and eventually reaching the Himalayas over 1,500 miles away.

In 2017, prior to the actual measurement work, the Department of Survey finalised the methodology for measuring Everest by taking the inputs of senior survey scientists from India, China, the US, and New Zealand, among other countries, some of which had previously been involved in measuring Everest’s height. In February 2018, Nepali surveyors started the precise levelling field survey from Maadar, Siraha, a Nepali district bordering India. Since Nepal doesn’t have direct access to sea-level data, the altitude of the sea level was derived from coordinates in the Bay of Bengal. Upon Nepal’s request, India collected sea-level data from the Bay of Bengal, and that data was linked with coordinates for Maadar—the Nepal-India border point. passages.text: Mount Everest Mount Everest (known in Nepali as Sagarmāthā[a], in Sherpa as Chamolangma[4], and in Tibetan as Jomolangma/Čhomolangma[b]) is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level. It lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas and marks part of the China–Nepal border at its summit.[5] Its height was most recently measured in 2020 through a joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities as 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8+1⁄2 in).[6][7] Mount Everest attracts many climbers, including highly experienced mountaineers. There are two main climbing routes, one approaching the summit from the southeast in Nepal (known as the standard route) and the other from the north in China. While not posing substantial technical climbing challenges on the standard route, Everest presents dangers such as altitude sickness, weather, and wind, as well as hazards from avalanches and the Khumbu Icefall. As of May 2024, 340 people have died on Everest. Over 200 bodies remain on the mountain and have not been removed due to the dangerous conditions.[8][9] Climbers typically ascend only part of Mount Everest's elevation, as the mountain's full elevation is measured from the geoid, which approximates sea level. Both governments agreed to recognise two separate heights, one based on rock and one on snow, with 8,848 m as the official figure and 8,844 m acknowledged as the rock height. Which Figure Should Be Used? Snow height, in almost every context. It is the convention applied to every other peak on Earth, since mountains are measured to their actual highest point rather than their bedrock, and it is the figure both governments announced jointly in December 2020. Rock height matters in two narrow cases: geological research tracking uplift and erosion, and comparisons where seasonal snow accumulation would distort the result. The 2020 joint survey never produced an agreed rock height, because Nepali and Chinese data on that measurement did not match and the two sides dropped that part of the collaboration. The 2005 figure of 8,844.43 m therefore remains the only rock height in circulation, and it is fifteen years older than the snow figure beside it. The Surveyor General published the result in 1856, identifying the peak then catalogued as Peak XV. Can Everest’s Summit Be Seen From Kathmandu? No. The ranges visible from Kathmandu Valley viewpoints are Langtang and Ganesh Himal. Everest sits too far east and is screened by closer peaks, which is why scenic mountain flights depart Kathmandu specifically to bring passengers within sight of it. Why Is Everest Measured in Meters With Decimals but Feet Without? The survey was conducted metrically, so 8,848.86 m is the measured value and every foot figure is a conversion. Quoting 29,031.7 ft implies a precision of a tenth of a foot that the original measurement does not claim, which is why most publications round to the nearest foot. The closest sea to Mount Everest's summit is the Bay of Bengal, almost 700 km (430 mi) away. To approximate a climb of the entire height of Mount Everest, one would need to start from this coastline, a feat accomplished by Tim Macartney-Snape's team in 1990. Climbers usually begin their ascent from base camps above 5,000 m (16,404 ft). The amount of elevation climbed from below these camps varies. On the Tibetan side, most climbers drive directly to the North Base Camp. On the Nepalese side, climbers generally fly into Kathmandu, then Lukla, and trek to the South Base Camp, making the climb from Lukla to the summit about 6,000 m (20,000 ft) in elevation gain. The first recorded efforts to reach Everest's summit were made by British mountaineers. As Nepal did not allow foreigners to enter the country at the time, the British made several attempts on the North Ridge route from the Tibetan side. passages.text: Mount Everest is 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 feet) above sea level. That figure was set on 8 December 2020, when Nepal and China jointly announced the result of the first survey the two countries had ever conducted and agreed on together. It replaced the 8,848 m figure that had stood since 1955, and it is the height recognised by both governments today. The number looks simple. Arriving at it took 164 years, six official revisions, a bilateral dispute over whether snow counts as part of a mountain, and a surveyor who lost a toe getting the reading. Key Takeaways - Official height: 8,848.86 m / 29,031.7 ft, or 29,031 feet 8.5 inches - Confirmed by the Nepal and China joint resurvey, announced December 2020 - This is the snow height. The rock beneath the summit snowcap sits at 8,844.43 m - Everest is the highest point above sea level, but not the tallest mountain measured base to summit - The peak is still rising by roughly 2 mm a year, faster than tectonics alone explains - Everest Base Camp sits at 5,364 m, and Kala Patthar at 5,545 m, around 63 percent of the summit altitude - Air at the summit

passages.text: Trigonometric Survey, a Herculean effort to survey the height of the world's tallest mountains, to measure the curvature of the Earth and mean sea level in British India. People "carried in" sea level , bringing the measurement done at the coast inland by marching miles and miles from the coast to Nepal with two bars. They measured the elevation change over a given ground distance by calculating the difference between the height of the two bars using a mounted, swiveling level, according to the Himalayan Club, a climbing and expedition club that provides scholarly information and history on the Himalayas. Nowadays, geographers use a mathematical expression to estimate sea level. They imagine what would happen if there were no winds or tides, and all the water from the seas could reach interior continental areas by means of tiny, narrow channels. This creates an idealized bumpy, irregularly shaped spheroid that represents mean sea level, called a geoid, from which elevations can then be measured, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. That figure has held since 8 December 2020, when Nepal and China accepted a single number for the first time in the mountain’s surveyed history, and it counts the snow cap the way climbers experience it rather than the bedrock underneath. The number is precise, but it is not permanent. The summit rises about 2 millimeters a year, and the next survey will almost certainly report something slightly different. What does not change is the scale. Base Camp reaches 61 percent of that height and already sits above the altitude where the body starts to struggle. The remaining 39 percent is where Everest stops being a destination and becomes a mountaineering problem.
